answer: A nuclear reactor is basically a very powerful kettle. Inside, the fuel is uranium, packed into metal tubes called fuel rods. When uranium atoms split apart, they give off a lot of heat, and each split breaks off tiny particles that go on to split more atoms, so the process keeps itself going [1]. Water around the fuel soaks up the heat and helps keep that splitting going steadily. Special rods can be pushed in to slow it down or pulled out to speed it up, a bit like a gas pedal and brake [1]. The heat turns water into steam, and the steam spins a turbine, a big fan-like wheel hooked up to a generator that makes electricity [1]. Thick walls keep the radiation safely inside.

sources.title: NUCLEAR 101: How Does a Nuclear Reactor Work? – U.S. Department of Energy
